steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for a paper presenting IL-Datasets, our toolkit for imitation learning that helps create datasets, train agents and benchmark them. Explain the problems researchers face and how the toolkit addresses them.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Collecting expert samples for IL is hard
- Expert quality and comparison issues
- Evaluating IL techniques in new datasets is time-consuming
- IL-Datasets toolkit and its pipeline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Collecting expert samples
  - IL techniques need expert samples to train agent
  - arduous: record humans or train new agent from scratch with another paradigm
  - new dataset per technique -> no evaluation consistency across IL approaches (cite)
- Expert quality
  - which experts collect data matters
  - usually no info about quality of collected data (cite) -> can drastically affect performance (cite)
  - researchers must find code and run it on each new dataset for consistent comparison
- Evaluating IL in new datasets is time-consuming
  - (i) not all techniques have code; (ii) implementations may have bugs; (iii) may not support user's environment
  - testbeds like Gym (cite) help with environment support
  - still up to researchers to support all environments: continuous/discrete actions and state spaces
- IL-Datasets (cite)
  - (i) creating datasets: faster multithreaded creation, curated expert policies
  - (ii) training: share readily available datasets, easily customisable data
  - (iii) benchmarking: results for IL techniques in diverse environments
  - Figure 1: pipeline stages
  - step (i): 'Controller' class, expert policies on HuggingFace (cite) or custom via 'Policy' interface
  - step (ii): 'BaselineDataset' for training/evaluation datasets (data from HuggingFace or local)
  - step (iii): benchmarking strategy (data, hyperparameters); no leakage (training data present during test); records details for reproducibility/comparison

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To create imitation learning (IL) techniques, researchers have to gather expert samples to train an agent in the task they want. This can be an arduous process, because collecting expert samples usually means either recording humans doing the task or training a new agent from scratch with some other learning paradigm. Also, when a new dataset is created for every new technique, there is no evaluation consistency across the different IL approaches.

We also have to think about which experts are used to collect the data when we create IL datasets. Most of the time when a new expert is created there is no information given about the quality of the collected data, and this can affect the performance across different IL approaches drastically. Researchers also have to find available code and run it on every newly created dataset to get a consistent comparison.

- Evaluating IL in new datasets is time-consuming
  - (i) code not always available; (ii) bugs; (iii) environment not supported
  - Gym helps with environment support, but researchers still need code for continuous/discrete action and state spaces
- IL-Datasets toolkit
  - (i) dataset creation (multithreaded, curated experts); (ii) training with shared customisable datasets; (iii) benchmarking in diverse environments
  - Figure 1 pipeline: 'Controller' + HuggingFace or custom 'Policy'; 'BaselineDataset'; benchmarking strategy, no leakage, details recorded

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To create imitation learning (IL) techniques, researchers have to gather expert samples to train an agent in the task they want. This can be an arduous process, because collecting expert samples usually means either recording humans doing the task or training a new agent from scratch with some other learning paradigm. Also, when a new dataset is created for every new technique, there is no evaluation consistency across the different IL approaches.

We also have to think about which experts are used to collect the data when we create IL datasets. Most of the time when a new expert is created there is no information given about the quality of the collected data, and this can affect the performance across different IL approaches drastically. Researchers also have to find available code and run it on every newly created dataset to get a consistent comparison.

It takes a lot of time to evaluate IL techniques in new datasets because: (i) not all techniques have code available; (ii) implementations can contain bugs; and (iii) published versions might not support the environment the user is experimenting with. Testbeds such as Gym help researchers with the problem of different environment support. But researchers still have to write code that supports all the available environments, such as ones with continuous and discrete actions and states spaces.

Because of these issues we developed Imitation Learning Datasets (IL-Datasets), a toolkit that tries to help researchers by: (i) creating new datasets, with faster multithreaded creation and curated expert policies; (ii) helping with training IL agents, by sharing readily available datasets with data that is easy to customise; and (iii) benchmarking, by giving results for IL techniques in a diverse set of environments. Figure 1 shows each stage in a typical pipeline implementation. In Step (i) users can use a 'Controller' class to create datasets with expert policies hosted on HuggingFace or custom ones that follow the 'Policy' interface. Once the dataset is selected (from the data on HuggingFace or locally), the user can instantiate the 'BaselineDataset' to create training and evaluation datasets and train an agent in step (ii). Finally, in step (iii) users can specify a benchmarking strategy, including data and hyperparameters, and the toolkit makes sure that no leakage happens (leakage means training data being present during test), and it records the benchmarking details for reproducibility and for better comparison with other work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Creating imitation learning (IL) techniques requires researchers to gather expert samples to train an agent in the desired task. This process can be arduous, since collecting expert samples usually involves either recording humans performing the task or training a new agent from scratch using another learning paradigm. Moreover, creating new datasets for each new technique does not allow for consistent evaluation across different IL approaches [1].

When creating IL datasets, we must also consider which experts are used to collect the data. Most often, when a new expert is created, no information is given about the quality of the data collected [2], which can drastically affect performance across different IL approaches [1]. Moreover, researchers must find available code and run it on any newly created dataset for a consistent comparison.

Evaluating IL techniques in new datasets is time-consuming because: (i) not all techniques have code readily available; (ii) implementations might contain bugs; and (iii) published versions might not support the environment the user is experimenting with. Testbeds such as Gym [3] help researchers overcome problems with different environment support. However, it is still up to researchers to write code that supports all available environments, such as those with continuous and discrete actions and states spaces.

In light of these issues, we have developed Imitation Learning Datasets (IL-Datasets) [4], a toolkit that aims to help researchers by: (i) creating new datasets through faster multithreaded creation and curated expert policies; (ii) assisting the training of IL agents by sharing readily available datasets with easily customisable data; and (iii) benchmarking by providing results for IL techniques in a diverse set of environments. Figure 1 shows each stage of a typical pipeline implementation. In Step (i) users can use a 'Controller' class to create datasets using expert policies hosted on HuggingFace [5] or custom-made ones that follow the 'Policy' interface. With the dataset selected (from the data provided on HuggingFace or locally), the user can instantiate the 'BaselineDataset' to create training and evaluation datasets and train an agent in step (ii). Lastly, in step (iii), users can specify a benchmarking strategy, including data and hyperparameters, and the toolkit will ensure that no leakage (training data being present during test) occurs, recording the benchmarking details for reproducibility and better comparison with other work.

References:
